h: The 1949 Nobel Prize in Medicine went to the inventor of the lobotomy.
d: Portuguese neurologist Egas Moniz shared the 1949 prize for developing the prefrontal leucotomy. It was performed on thousands of patients before better drugs arrived, and calls to revoke the prize have never succeeded.

s.t: The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 1949

h: To prove yellow fever was not contagious, a trainee doctor smeared patients' vomit into his own cuts.
d: Stubbins Ffirth was sure the disease came from summer heat, not contact, so he experimented on himself, even pouring the fluid onto his eyeballs. He was right that it peaks in summer but wrong about the cause, which turned out to be mosquitoes.

h: A Scottish man went 382 days without solid food in 1965, and it was a medical record.
d: Angus Barbieri checked into a Dundee hospital for a short fast but insisted on continuing because he adapted so well. He lived on tea, coffee, sparkling water, vitamins and yeast extract, and fell from about 207 kg to about 82 kg.

h: About 1.7 billion years ago, a uranium deposit in Gabon ran as a natural nuclear reactor.
d: Oklo, discovered in 1972, remains the only known place where this happened, across sixteen sites. The reactions switched on and off for a few hundred thousand years, probably never exceeding 100 kW of thermal power, long before humans built one.

h: Bayer sold heroin as a non-addictive cough medicine.
d: Bayer marketed diacetylmorphine over the counter under the trademark Heroin from 1898 to 1910, as a morphine substitute for cough suppressants. Morphine was a popular recreational drug, and Bayer wanted a non-addictive alternative. Instead, heroin soon had one of the highest addiction rates among its users.

h: Dynamite's inventor was prescribed nitroglycerin for his heart.
d: A few months before he died in 1896, Alfred Nobel was prescribed nitroglycerin for his heart condition. He wrote to a friend about the irony of fate, noting it was sold as Trinitrin so as not to scare the chemist and the public. Doctors used the name glyceryl trinitrate for the same reason.

h: One catacomb in Egypt held nearly 8 million animal mummies, most of them dogs.
d: Pilgrims at Saqqara dedicated the mummies to Anubis, the jackal-headed god of death, and animal breeders nearby likely raised the dogs for the purpose. Grave robbers and industrialists later disturbed much of the catacomb, and many of the mummies were probably ground into fertilizer.

s.t: 8 Million Dog Mummies Found in 'God of Death' Mass Grave

h: Emperor Vespasian taxed Rome's public toilets, then made his son sniff the money.
d: When Titus complained about the tax, Vespasian held a coin from the first payment to his son's nose and asked whether the smell offended him. Titus said no. "Yet it comes from urine," the emperor replied. The Roman biographer Suetonius recorded it among Vespasian's jokes about his unpopular ways of raising money.

s.t: The Life of Vespasian, 23 (Lives of the Caesars, Loeb translation)

h: Oxford University is older than the Aztec Empire.
d: Teaching in Oxford had begun by 1096. The Aztecs founded their capital, Tenochtitlán, now Mexico City, in 1325, and their empire took shape through an alliance in 1428 before falling to Spanish forces in 1521. The White House has been standing longer than the Aztecs ruled from their capital.

s.t: The University of Oxford Is Older Than the Aztec Empire and Other Facts That Will Change Your Perspective on History

h: Sweden once had a February 30th, in 1712.
d: Sweden tried to switch calendars gradually by skipping leap days from 1700, then forgot in 1704 and 1708, leaving it out of step with everyone. King Charles XII ordered a return to the old calendar, adding a second extra day to 1712. Sweden finally adopted the modern calendar in 1753.

h: In 1518, people in Strasbourg danced for days without stopping, and hundreds joined in.
d: The dancing plague began in July 1518 when one woman started dancing in the street. Within weeks about 400 people had joined, and some reportedly collapsed from exhaustion. Officials even hired musicians, wrongly thinking more dancing would cure it. Its cause is still debated.

h: One man survived both atomic bombs: Hiroshima, then Nagasaki three days later.
d: Tsutomu Yamaguchi was in Hiroshima on business on August 6, 1945, was injured, and went home to Nagasaki. On August 9 he was in his office there when the second bomb fell. Japan officially recognized him as a double survivor in 2009. He died in 2010 at 93.

h: In 1919 a wave of molasses swept through Boston at about 35 miles an hour and killed 21 people.
d: On January 15, 1919 a storage tank burst in Boston's North End, releasing more than 2 million gallons of molasses. A wave several feet high crushed buildings and dragged people under. Twenty-one died, and the neighborhood reportedly smelled of molasses for decades.

h: The US and Britain nearly went to war in 1859 over a dead pig.
d: A farmer shot a British-owned pig rooting in his garden on San Juan Island, which both nations claimed. Troops massed on both sides. The only casualty of the 1859 crisis was the pig. The dispute was settled by arbitration, and the island became American in 1872.

h: In 897 a pope put his dead predecessor's corpse on trial.
d: Pope Stephen VI had Formosus dug up in 897, dressed in papal robes and sat on a throne to answer charges. The "Cadaver Synod" found him guilty, cut off the fingers he used for blessings, and threw the body in the Tiber. Later popes annulled it.

h: In 1386 a French court hanged a pig for murder, after dressing it in human clothes.
d: In Falaise, Normandy, a sow was convicted of killing a baby and sentenced to be mutilated and hanged in public. Medieval and early modern Europe held hundreds of formal trials of animals, complete with lawyers assigned to defend them.

h: In AD 193 the Roman Empire's throne was sold at auction, and Didius Julianus won it.
d: The auction was run by the Praetorian Guard, who had just assassinated the previous emperor, Pertinax. Julianus reigned only from March to June 193. Septimius Severus marched on Rome, and Julianus, abandoned by the Senate and the Guard, was killed in the palace.

h: In medieval Europe, ground-up Egyptian mummies were sold as medicine.
d: The word began as a Persian bitumen, mumia, thought to cure almost anything. Around the 12th century, when imported bitumen ran short, it was misread as "mummy", and merchants started shipping real mummies from Egypt. When Egypt banned the trade in the 16th century, apothecaries began faking them.

h: Violet Jessop survived the Titanic, its sister ship the Britannic, and a collision aboard the Olympic.
d: Jessop was a stewardess, nicknamed Miss Unsinkable. She was aboard RMS Olympic when it collided with HMS Hawke in 1911, survived the Titanic sinking in 1912, and survived the sinking of HMHS Britannic in 1916, where she was working as a nurse.

h: Flight attendant Vesna Vulovic fell about 10,160 metres without a parachute and survived.
d: She was the only survivor of JAT Flight 367, which crashed in Czechoslovakia in 1972 after an explosion. She spent days in a coma and was temporarily paralyzed from the waist down, but recovered almost fully. She remembered little of it and had no fear of flying afterward.

h: Artists painted with a brown pigment made from ground-up Egyptian mummies.
d: Mummy brown was made from mummy flesh mixed with white pitch and myrrh. It was hugely popular with Western European artists from the mid-eighteenth century, and Delacroix and the Pre-Raphaelites used it. Demand collapsed by 1915 as fresh mummies grew scarce and artists disliked its finish.

h: A sound recorded before 1861 sat unplayable until 2008, when a computer finally read it.
d: The recordings were made on a phonautograph, which traced sound waves as a line on smoke-blackened paper. It was built only to look at sound, not replay it. In 2008 the tracings were scanned optically and processed into digital audio, revealing the voices for the first time.

h: In 1726 a woman convinced doctors she was giving birth to rabbits.
d: Mary Toft of Godalming fooled the surgeon John Howard and even Nathaniel St. André, surgeon to King George I. Brought to London and studied closely, she confessed to the hoax. The scandal ruined several surgeons' careers, and Hogarth mocked the gullible medical profession.

h: Vikings' horned helmets come from 1800s opera, not history.
d: The image was popularized by Richard Wagner's Norse operas, which put horns and wings on Viking helmets. Contemporary Viking Age texts mention helmets but never horned ones, and the few period helmets found so far do not have horns either.

h: A single slime mold, with no brain, recreated the Tokyo rail network in 26 hours.
d: Researchers in 2010 placed oat flakes in the pattern of cities around Tokyo and let Physarum polycephalum grow. Its tube network matched the real rail system in efficiency and resilience to breaks, though it has no nervous system.

h: This sea slug steals chloroplasts from the algae it eats and runs on photosynthesis.
d: Elysia chlorotica belongs to a group of sap-sucking sea slugs that use chloroplasts from the algae they eat, a phenomenon called kleptoplasty. The stolen chloroplasts turn its body bright green, which also works as camouflage against predators.

h: Mike the Headless Chicken lived for 18 months after his head was cut off.
d: Farmer Lloyd Olsen's axe missed the jugular vein and left most of the brain stem intact, and a blood clot stopped the bleeding. Mike became nationally famous, and his hometown of Fruita, Colorado, still holds a Mike the Headless Chicken Day every May.

h: The binturong, an Asian bearcat, gives off a popcorn smell from its musk glands.
d: The binturong lives in the trees of South and Southeast Asia and has a long, bushy, prehensile tail. Its popcorn-scented musk glands are unique to it. Females can also delay implantation, holding a fertilized egg until conditions are ideal.

h: The hairy frog can push retractable claws out through its skin.
d: Also called the horror frog, this Central African species has hair-like skin growths on the flanks and thighs of breeding males. They contain arteries and are thought to help absorb oxygen while the male guards his eggs in the water.

h: Sony's PlayStation began as a failed CD-ROM add-on for Nintendo's Super Nintendo.
d: In the early 1990s Sony worked with Nintendo on a CD-ROM peripheral for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System, but the venture failed. Sony began developing its own console after that. It was released in Japan on 3 December 1994 and competed with the Nintendo 64 and the Sega Saturn.

h: A doctor showed premature babies in a Coney Island sideshow, and it saved over 6,500 of them.
d: Martin Couney's "Infantorium" charged visitors 25 cents to see premature babies in incubators. At the time, premature babies were widely believed to be weaklings unfit to survive into adulthood. His sideshows are credited with saving the lives of over 6,500 of them.

h: Toy Story 2 nearly vanished in 1998 when a mistaken command wiped 90% of it.
d: An animator clearing files entered the deletion command /bin/rm -r -f * on the root folder of the film's assets. The backups had not been working for about a month. The film was saved when technical director Galyn Susman, working from home with her newborn child, turned out to have a copy on her home computer.

h: The story of 38 neighbors who watched Kitty Genovese die and did nothing was wrong.
d: The 1964 New York Times story shaped how psychology taught the bystander effect. A 2007 review found no evidence for 38 witnesses, or that they saw the murder, or that they stayed inactive; the Times later called its own reporting flawed.

h: In 1962, a laughing fit spread through a Tanzanian girls' school and closed it for months.
d: It began with three girls on January 30 and reached 95 of the school's 159 pupils, aged 12 to 18. Symptoms lasted anywhere from a few hours to 16 days. The school closed on March 18, and the outbreak then spread to nearby villages and other schools.

h: The pathologist who autopsied Einstein kept his brain, and cut it into 170 pieces.
d: Thomas Harvey performed the autopsy at Princeton Hospital in 1955, then preserved the brain on the condition that it be studied. He sectioned it into 170 pieces over three months and made 12 sets of slides. The brain weighed 1,230 grams, well within the normal human range.

h: France spans more time zones than any other country: 12, one more than Russia.
d: Its overseas territories do the work, from French Guiana to Réunion to New Caledonia. Tahiti runs at UTC−10 and Wallis and Futuna at UTC+12, so when it is 10 a.m. in Tahiti it is already 8 a.m. the next day in Wallis. Daylight saving in Saint Pierre and Miquelon adds a 13th zone for part of the year.

s.t: Country with the most time zones

h: Until 2015, one Indian field sat inside Bangladesh inside India inside Bangladesh.
d: Dahala Khagrabari was the world's only third-order enclave until it was ceded to Bangladesh on 1 August 2015. It covered 7,000 square metres, about a football field, and was farmland where nobody lived. Its owner was a Bangladeshi farmer who lived in the enclave around it.

h: In 1980 a drill pierced a salt mine under Lake Peigneur, and the whole lake drained away.
d: An oil rig drilling for Texaco on November 20, 1980 punched into the Diamond Crystal Salt Company mine below. The hole formed a vortex that emptied the lake into caverns left by the removal of salt. The lake had been 10 feet deep; it is now the deepest lake in Louisiana, at 200 feet.

h: DNA was first discovered in 1869, in pus from used hospital bandages.
d: Swiss scientist Friedrich Miescher wanted white blood cells, and pus is full of them. From their nuclei he isolated a new substance he called nuclein. His 1871 paper, titled "On the Chemical Composition of Pus Cells," buried its significance until page 19 of 20, and the find was largely overlooked for decades.

s.t: The discovery of DNA started with this overlooked scientist

h: Your body gives off visible light, but it is about 1,000 times too faint for your eyes to see.
d: In 2009, researchers in Japan photographed five men in complete darkness with a camera cooled to minus 120°C. The glow was strongest around the cheeks and mouth, and it rose and fell through the day, peaking around 4 p.m. It likely comes from chemical reactions in the body's energy metabolism.

s.t: Imaging of Ultraweak Spontaneous Photon Emission from Human Body Displaying Diurnal Rhythm

h: Old church windows are thicker at the bottom, but not because glass slowly flows.
d: Calculations based on Westminster Abbey windows from 1268 show medieval glass flows at most about 1 nanometer in a billion years. The uneven panes come from how they were made: glass was blown, flattened and spun into disks of uneven thickness, and glaziers naturally set the heavy edge at the bottom.

s.t: Glass viscosity calculations definitively debunk the myth of observable flow in medieval windows

h: Gallium is a metal that melts in your hand, at about 85 degrees Fahrenheit.
d: Gallium melts at 29.76°C (85.6°F), so a solid lump turns to liquid in a warm palm or a cup of hot tea. It is used in blue LEDs and phone chips, and a gallium spoon is a classic party trick that leaves the spoon stub in your tea.

h: The Large Hadron Collider is colder than outer space.
d: Its magnets are chilled to 1.9 kelvin, or minus 271.3°C, using about 120 tonnes of liquid helium, colder than the 2.7 kelvin of deep space. That makes the 27-kilometer ring one of the coldest places in the universe, even as its collisions become the hottest.

h: A doctor drank a beaker of bacteria to prove they cause stomach ulcers.
d: Barry Marshall swallowed Helicobacter pylori and developed gastritis within days, to answer skeptics who insisted no bacterium could live in stomach acid. He and Robin Warren won the 2005 Nobel Prize, overturning the belief that ulcers came from stress and spicy food.

s.t: The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2005

h: Vikings were cutting trees in Canada in 1021, and a solar storm is how we know the exact year.
d: A burst of cosmic radiation in 993 left a radiocarbon spike in tree rings worldwide. Counting rings out from that spike in wood cut with metal tools at L'Anse aux Meadows, Newfoundland, showed all three trees were felled in 1021. It is the only secure date for Europeans in the Americas before Columbus.

s.t: Evidence for European presence in the Americas in AD 1021

h: The shortest recorded war ended in about 38 minutes, when Britain shelled Zanzibar in 1896.
d: In August 1896 a new sultan seized the palace in Zanzibar without British approval. A Royal Navy squadron gave an ultimatum, then opened fire at 9:00 a.m. The palace was wrecked, the sultan fled, and the fighting was over in roughly 38 minutes, the shortest war on record.

h: A Japanese soldier kept fighting World War II in the Philippine jungle until 1974.
d: Hiroo Onoda was sent to Lubang Island in 1944 and ignored leaflets saying the war was over, suspecting a trick. He only surrendered in 1974, after his former commanding officer flew in to formally relieve him of duty. That was nearly three decades after Japan's surrender.

h: The US bought Alaska in 1867 for $7.2 million, about two cents an acre.
d: Russia sold Alaska to the United States in 1867 for $7.2 million, a sum that critics at the time thought absurd. They called the deal "Seward's Folly" after Secretary of State William Seward. Gold, oil and fisheries later made it look like one of history's great bargains.

h: A volcano in Indonesia cancelled summer in 1816, and helped inspire Frankenstein.
d: Mount Tambora erupted in April 1815, and the ash and sulfur cooled the planet. In 1816 Europe and North America had crop failures and a cold, rainy June. Stuck indoors at Lake Geneva that summer, Mary Shelley began writing Frankenstein.

h: The Dutch once kept a tiny nutmeg island and handed over Manhattan in exchange.
d: In the 1667 Treaty of Breda, the Dutch confirmed control of Run, a speck in Indonesia's Banda Islands that was then a prime source of nutmeg. In return they gave up their claim to New Amsterdam, later renamed New York.

h: Mantis shrimp have 12 color receptors to our 3, but are worse than us at telling colors apart.
d: University of Queensland researchers trained the shrimp to pick a color for a food reward, then swapped in other colors to find the limits of their vision. Instead of blending signals from a few receptors as our brains do, theirs seem hard-wired to specific wavelengths: less subtle, but likely much faster on a crowded coral reef.

s.t: Study finds mantis shrimp process vision differently than other organisms

h: A raindrop can weigh 50 times as much as a mosquito, yet mosquitoes survive direct hits.
d: A mosquito is so light that a falling drop barely slows when it strikes, so little force passes to the insect. It rides the front of the drop for up to 20 body lengths, then uses its long legs and wings to twist free before it is driven into the ground. Scaled up to human size, one researcher said, the hit would be like being struck by a car.

s.t: Mosquitoes fly in rain thanks to low mass

h: A Venus flytrap counts: it snaps shut on the second touch and starts digesting on the fifth.
d: The first two touches on its trigger hairs have to come within about 30 seconds of each other. After that, every struggle of the trapped insect trips the hairs again, and the more it struggles, the more nitrogen-rich digestive enzymes the plant pours in. A team in Germany described the counting in Current Biology in 2016.

s.t: The Venus Flytrap Can Count Past 2

h: A wood frog can freeze solid: its heart stops and up to 65 percent of its body water turns to ice.
d: In winter it stops breathing and its heartbeat halts. Glucose flooding its cells acts like antifreeze, protecting them from damage. When spring warms the ice, the frog's heart restarts and it hops away, several days after thawing.

h: The golden poison frog carries enough toxin in its skin to kill about 10 adult humans.
d: Just 2 micrograms of batrachotoxin can be fatal. The frog does not make it: in the wild it takes the toxin from the beetles it eats, and captive-raised frogs on a different diet are harmless. Its bright yellow color warns predators to stay away.

h: A giraffe has just 7 neck vertebrae, the same number as a human.
d: Almost all mammals have seven, from mice to whales. A giraffe's are each more than 28 centimeters long, and its neck can be around 2 meters. A tiny bone difference in a sloth or manatee is the rare exception.

h: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon, and about 400 times farther away.
d: That is why the two look the same size in our sky, and why the Moon can cover the Sun exactly in a total eclipse. It will not last: the Moon's orbit grows about 3.8 cm a year, and in more than 600 million years it will be too far away to ever cover the Sun completely.

s.t: How Is the Sun Completely Blocked in an Eclipse?

h: A day on Venus is longer than its year.
d: Venus turns so slowly that one rotation takes about 243 Earth days, while its trip around the Sun takes about 225. It also spins backward compared with most planets, so on Venus the Sun rises in the west and sets in the east.

h: Humans have lived in space without a break since November 2, 2000.
d: Crews have occupied the International Space Station continuously since Expedition 1 arrived that day. Every person born since then has grown up on a planet with people orbiting above it at all times. Every person born since then has grown up with people orbiting overhead.

h: The Apollo missions brought back 382 kilograms of Moon rock, and some of it is still sealed unopened.
d: Six landings returned 842 pounds of rock, core samples and soil. NASA has kept some samples sealed for decades, so future scientists can study them with tools that do not exist yet. A great deal of it was collected for tests that scientists had not yet invented.

h: Saturn's moon Enceladus sprays jets of ocean water into space.
d: Cassini flew through the plumes and found water, salts and organic molecules coming from a global ocean beneath the ice. The moon is only about 500 kilometers wide, yet it feeds one of Saturn's rings.

h: You could fit about 1.3 million Earths inside the Sun.
d: The Sun is 99.8 percent of the solar system's mass, but it is mostly empty volume: it would take 1.3 million Earths to fill it, yet only about 330,000 Earths to match its mass. The Sun is so huge that its gravity holds every planet in orbit.

h: The first message on the internet's ancestor, ARPANET, was "lo": the system crashed mid-"login."
d: At 10:30 p.m. on October 29, 1969, UCLA student Charley Kline tried to log in to a computer at the Stanford Research Institute over the brand-new ARPANET. The "l" and the "o" made it across, then the system crashed. His supervisor, Leonard Kleinrock, puts it this way: the first message was "lo," as in "lo and behold." The full login worked about an hour later.

s.t: The Day the Infant Internet Uttered its First Words

h: The fax machine was patented in 1843, well before the telephone.
d: Scottish clockmaker Alexander Bain's design sent images over telegraph wires. Giovanni Caselli's pantelegraph opened a commercial service between Paris and Lyon in 1865. Fax machines only spread to ordinary offices in the 1980s, more than a century later.

h: The first text message, sent on December 3, 1992, said "Merry Christmas."
d: Engineer Neil Papworth typed it on a computer and sent it to Vodafone director Richard Jarvis's handset. Jarvis could not reply, because phones of the day had no way to type a text. It took years for texting to catch on.

h: Microsoft included Solitaire in Windows to help people learn to use a mouse.
d: Microsoft intended Solitaire to soothe people intimidated by the operating system. Many users were still unfamiliar with graphical interfaces, so moving cards taught them the drag-and-drop technique. It was programmed by an intern, Wes Cherry, in the summer of 1988.

h: In 1996 AOL's profanity filter stopped the people of Scunthorpe from creating accounts.
d: The English town's name contains a string of letters that the filter read as obscene. Computers find text easily but struggle with context, so broad blocking rules catch innocent words. The mistake gave its name to the Scunthorpe problem.

h: The Matrix's falling green code is not made of sushi recipes, despite what its designer joked.
d: Designer Simon Whiteley said in a 2017 interview that the code was sushi recipes, but this has been debunked. His custom typeface actually uses mirrored half-width Japanese kana mixed with Western letters and numerals.

h: Swap a stranger for someone else mid-conversation, and about half of people won't notice.
d: In a 1998 experiment, a researcher stopped people on a college campus to ask for directions. Two people carrying a wooden door walked between them, and in that moment a different researcher took his place and carried on talking. About half kept giving directions as if nothing had happened, and many missed it even when the two researchers wore different-colored clothes.

s.t: Memory for centrally attended changing objects in an incidental real-world change detection paradigm (Levin, Simons, Angelone & Chabris, British Journal of Psychology, 2002)

h: A placebo labeled as a placebo still eased irritable bowel symptoms: 59% improved versus 35%.
d: In a 2010 trial, 80 patients with irritable bowel syndrome were told plainly that their pills were inert sugar pills, then took them twice a day for three weeks. Adequate symptom relief was reported by 59% of them, compared with 35% of patients who got no pills.

s.t: Placebos without Deception: A Randomized Controlled Trial in Irritable Bowel Syndrome

h: In 1913, a Monte Carlo roulette wheel landed on black 26 times in a row.
d: That streak gave the gambler's fallacy its other name, the Monte Carlo fallacy. It is the mistaken belief that a rare run makes the opposite result more likely next. But each spin is independent: a fair die still has a 1 in 6 chance of a '4' on every single roll.

h: The creator of Wonder Woman also invented an early prototype of the lie detector.
d: William Moulton Marston was a Harvard-trained psychologist who, with his wife Elizabeth Holloway, built an early polygraph. He also wrote self-help books and comics. His wife and their partner Olive Byrne greatly influenced Wonder Woman's creation, and he entered the Comic Book Hall of Fame in 2006.

h: Some expectant fathers gain weight and get morning sickness alongside their pregnant partners.
d: Couvade syndrome, also called sympathetic pregnancy, is a proposed condition in which a non-pregnant partner shares the symptoms: weight gain, nausea and disturbed sleep. In extreme cases it includes labor pains. Its cause is debated, with some pointing to psychology and others to hormone changes.

h: On 19th-century Martha's Vineyard, hearing and deaf islanders alike spoke in sign language.
d: Martha's Vineyard Sign Language was used from the early 18th century to 1952. In 1854, one islander in 155 was deaf, against about one in 5,730 nationally. In one part of Chilmark, as many as 1 in 4 of the 60 residents was deaf, so nearly everyone signed.

h: Every continent on Earth could fit inside the Pacific Ocean at once.
d: The Pacific holds more than half of all the free water on the planet, and it is the deepest ocean basin as well as the largest. It is also the oldest, with its oldest rocks dated to about 200 million years, and its rim is the Ring of Fire, where plates slide under one another and set off earthquakes and eruptions.

s.t: What is the largest ocean basin on Earth?

h: The summit farthest from Earth's center isn't Everest. It's Chimborazo, in Ecuador.
d: Earth's spin makes it bulge at the Equator, and Chimborazo sits just one degree south of it. Its peak is 6,268 meters above sea level, far below Everest's 8,848, yet it is more than 2,000 meters farther from the planet's center. Everest is the highest point above sea level; Chimborazo is the closest point on Earth to the stars.

s.t: What is the highest point on Earth as measured from Earth's center?

h: Pheasant Island belongs to France for six months a year and to Spain for the other six.
d: France administers the uninhabited river island from 1 August to 31 January, and Spain takes over from 1 February to 31 July. Despite the name, there are no pheasants on it. It is where the Treaty of the Pyrenees was signed in 1659, after 24 conferences between Spanish and French ministers.

h: China built a full-scale replica of the Austrian town of Hallstatt.
d: It was reported on 2 June 2012 that the Chinese mining company China Minmetals Corporation had built a full-scale replica of the entire town in Huizhou, in Guangdong province. Hallstatt is actually twinned with Huizhou, and the copy later appeared in a 2022 episode of the Korean series Money Heist: Korea.

h: The 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake shortened Earth's day by 2.68 microseconds.
d: The earthquake shifted mass inside the Earth. It displaced the North Pole by 25 mm and slightly changed the planet's shape, decreasing Earth's oblateness by about one part in 10 billion. That sped up Earth's rotation a little, which shortened the day.
